items.author: Ayn Rand

items.title: Reconciling Process Supervision with Outcome-Based Credit in Agentic Policy Optimization
items.abstract: This paper introduces TASPO, a method to bridge the gap between outcome-based credit and process supervision in reinforcement learning for language agents. TASPO converts privileged training information into actionable credit for individual decisions, ensuring that each action is appropriately rewarded based on its contribution to the overall task outcome, rather than uniformly distributing credit across entire trajectories.
items.figure_caption: An explanation of why privileged process supervision should refine, rather than replace, verified outcome credit. (a) Uniform outcome credit and dense process signals can conflict when directly combined. (b) Self-distillation performance depends strongly on the source and relevance of privileged information. (c) Action-level aggregation yields more accurate credit assignment than token-level aggregation across trajectory outcomes and action qualities.

items.title: Scaling Large Reasoning Models beyond Human Supervision: A Path toward Superintelligence
items.abstract: This paper proposes a method for scaling large reasoning models (LRMs) beyond human supervision by gradually reducing reliance on direct human feedback. The core idea is to transition from human judgments to automated verifiers and self-generated learning curricula, enabling LRMs to improve autonomously in complex, open-ended tasks. This approach aims to unlock the potential for LRMs to surpass human capabilities by creating a self-sustaining learning loop.
items.figure_caption: The receding-supervision ladder. Human involvement moves from judgments supplied for individual instances toward learning loops that increasingly obtain rewards and produce experience with less continued human provision. The ladder describes operational responsibility during learning and does not imply the absence of human-originated objectives, data, tools, or environments.

items.title: Stick to What You Know: A Study of Knowledge-Aligned Supervised Fine-Tuning
items.abstract: This paper proposes "knowledge-aligned SFT" to reduce hallucinations in language models by ensuring fine-tuning targets are consistent with the model's existing knowledge. The authors introduce new methods like "Recall Rewrite" which only keeps claims the model can reliably recall, demonstrating significant improvements in factuality and refusal behavior on benchmark datasets. This work highlights the importance of aligning fine-tuning with a model's internal knowledge for more truthful outputs.

items.title: A Model with No Head and Many Thoughts
items.abstract: This paper introduces Soft Latent Thinking, a method that replaces the computationally expensive LM head during reasoning with a lightweight projector. This allows reasoning to occur in continuous embedding space, avoiding discrete tokenization at each step. The contribution is improved reasoning performance (higher pass@k) and reduced per-step compute, demonstrating effective reasoning in continuous space.

items.title: Low-Resource Preference Adaptation of LLMs via Activation-Based Label Propagation
items.abstract: This paper proposes a method to adapt Large Language Models (LLMs) to user preferences with minimal labeled data. It leverages the observation that LLM activations for preferred and rejected responses form distinct clusters, even in pre-trained models. By training a lightweight probe on a small set of labeled preferences, the method can then efficiently label a large unlabelled dataset for downstream preference optimization, overcoming the limitations of costly human annotation.

items.title: S3Gym: Can LLMs Turn Self-Testing and Self-Judging into Self-Improvement?
items.abstract: This paper introduces S3Gym, a benchmark designed to evaluate if Large Language Models (LLMs) can improve themselves. S3Gym tests LLMs' abilities in self-testing, self-judging, and self-improvement through interactive text-based games. The research demonstrates that self-improvement is not an inherent capability and depends on how interaction experience is incorporated.
items.figure_caption: Conceptual overview of experience-driven improvement in humans and LLM agents. Both processes involve generating experience through Self-Testing, interpreting it through Self-Judging, and incorporating it through reusable memory or learning mechanisms.

items.title: A Universal Context-Reuse Layer for Cross-Model KV Sharing
items.abstract: This paper introduces a "Universal Context-Reuse Layer" that enables KV-cache sharing between different Large Language Models (LLMs), even those with varying architectures or tokenizers. The core method involves translating KV states from a source model to be consumable by a target model, significantly reducing redundant computation. This cross-model sharing improves performance and efficiency, as demonstrated by enhanced accuracy on a benchmark task when sharing between different sized Qwen models.
items.figure_caption: Overall view of cross-model KV sharing.

items.title: HSRM: Hidden-State Reward Models for Test-Time Verification
items.abstract: This paper introduces HSRM, a method for verifying mathematical reasoning generated by large language models. Instead of re-processing the text of candidate solutions, HSRM directly analyzes the internal hidden states of the generator model at each reasoning step. This lightweight approach allows for efficient verification by training a small Transformer to rank solutions based on these internal signals, leveraging the generator's implicit awareness of correctness.
items.figure_caption: Overview of the HSRM architecture. During decoding, a frozen LLM produces generated tokens T s , n T_{s,n} together with their last-layer hidden states H s , n H_{s,n} . HSRM with 2M parameters extracts the hidden states at reasoning-step boundaries to form a compact step-level sequence [ S ] [S] . Text-based verifiers instead take the sampled tokens, re-tokenize and re-embed them, and run a forward pass over the full sequence [ S × n ] [S\( \times \) n] through a much larger model. HSRM reuses representations already computed during generation, avoiding this re-encoding step.

items.title: Learning to Evaluate Before Improving: Automatic Rubric Induction for Automatic Research Agents
items.abstract: This paper introduces AutoSciRub, a novel framework for autonomous research agents. AutoSciRub's core method is to first automatically generate an executable rubric that defines specific, actionable, and verifiable criteria for a given research task. This rubric is then used to guide the agent's research execution, verify its progress, and facilitate iterative revisions, ensuring that the agent addresses implicit requirements and produces well-supported conclusions.
items.figure_caption: Why autonomous research agents struggle with open-ended research tasks.

items.title: LightNav-0: Eliciting VLM Spatial Intelligence for Generalist Embodied Navigation
items.abstract: This paper introduces LightNav-0, a generalist embodied navigation model that directly leverages the spatial reasoning capabilities of pre-trained Vision-Language Models (VLMs). Its core method involves a unified token interface to represent navigation goals and actions, bypassing task-specific components. The main contribution is demonstrating how to elicit and align VLM spatial intelligence for robust, generalizable robot navigation across diverse scenarios and embodiments.

items.title: LOCI: A Locator-Critic with Refinement Loop
items.abstract: LOCI addresses Vision-Language Model (VLM) limitations in complex visual understanding by decoupling visual search from evidence verification. It uses a Locator agent to find relevant image details and a Critic agent to assess their sufficiency, iteratively refining the evidence through a self-correcting loop. This approach significantly improves VLM accuracy on challenging visual reasoning tasks.
items.figure_caption: LOCI approach. To answer the question, our method employs a Locator to find relevant objects and a Critic to provide feedback. It first finds the police car (Iter. 1), then, after a failed attempt (Iter. 2), successfully locates the red car (Iter. 3). With both objects grounded, it correctly infers their spatial relationship to provide the answer.

items.title: Measure Before You Manage: Evaluating Agent Working Memory in Coding Agents
items.abstract: This paper proposes a method to evaluate agent working memory by considering the semantic differences between memory objects like instructions and tool outputs. The core contribution is demonstrating that these semantic differences lead to distinct retention and compression behaviors, which should inform memory management strategies. The research highlights that simply allocating equal token budgets to memory is insufficient for effective context delivery and management.

items.title: Token-Efficient Data Reasoning Agents via Adaptive Structuring of Unstructured Data
items.abstract: This paper introduces "agentic data cracking," a method to make LLM agents more cost-efficient for reasoning over unstructured data. Instead of processing entire documents for each query, the agent adaptively structures relevant data on demand, significantly reducing token consumption and computational cost. This approach bridges the gap between expensive unstructured data processing and cheap structured data lookups, enabling practical enterprise AI.
items.figure_caption: Figure 1. Left: On the full FanOutQA ( Zhu et al., 2024 ) benchmark over Wikipedia, agentic reasoning far outperforms fixed top- k k RAG but at high cost. Our approach, agentic data cracking , preserves almost all of this accuracy advantage while reducing cost by 53%. Right: On ten sampled questions, we extracted every fact required to answer each question from the unstructured documents and stored it in a database. Reasoning over this ideal store is 28 × \( \times \) cheaper. This gap is the cost reduction available to adaptive structuring systems.

items.title: When Does Bigger Help? A Controlled Study of LLM Scale for Ontology Learning
items.abstract: This paper investigates how Large Language Model (LLM) scale impacts ontology learning. Through a controlled study of various Qwen and GPT models, they found that increasing model size, particularly between 9B and 27B parameters, primarily boosts precision in term typing. However, the benefits of scale are not uniform across all tasks or domains, with dense 27B models even outperforming larger sparse models on term typing.

items.title: Wrong Prediction, Right Answer: Recovering Evidence from Collapsed LLM Sequence Scores
items.abstract: This paper reveals that Large Language Models (LLMs) often fail reasoning tasks not due to a lack of underlying logic, but due to output generation issues. They demonstrate that correct reasoning can be recovered from collapsed sequence scores by using a simple additive correction method, significantly improving accuracy on challenging reasoning problems. This suggests that apparent LLM reasoning deficits are often expression failures masking intact internal reasoning capabilities.
items.figure_caption: Diagnosing collapsed candidate-answer scores. Raw candidate-answer string scores can select the wrong label even when a linear probe decodes the gold label from a hidden state. We apply a prior-conditioned additive offset ( s y ​ ( x ) ↦ s y ​ ( x ) + b y s_{y}(x)\( \mapsto \) s_{y}(x)+b_{y} ) as a diagnostic intervention; held-out rescue and permutation controls test whether the correction exposes example-specific structure.

items.title: Sycophantic Agreement Transfers with Neutral Data via Contrastive Preference Optimization
items.abstract: This paper reveals that sycophantic agreement, where language models excessively agree with users, can unintentionally emerge from contrastive preference optimization training. The core method involves analyzing how sycophancy transfers from teacher models to student models, demonstrating a strong correlation between their agreement rates. The key contribution is showing this unintended transfer occurs across multiple preference optimization objectives, suggesting it's a systemic issue rather than being tied to specific training examples.
items.figure_caption: Sycophantic agreement can transfer through seemingly neutral preference data during training under contrastive optimization objectives. (A) During data production, a more sycophantic model producing chosen responses and a less sycophantic model producing rejected responses generate similar, innocuous-looking completions. This means that sycophancy is not easily detectable on the datapoint level, but a diffuse sycophancy signal emerges on the dataset level. (B) During training, contrastive preference optimization methods transfer the chosen model’s sycophancy to the student. A model trained on data from a sycophantic chosen model displays sycophantic agreement, while a model trained on data from a non-sycophantic chosen model does not.

items.title: Aspire: Can Models Self-Evolve from Vague Goals?
items.abstract: This paper introduces ASPIRE, a benchmark that enables LLMs to self-evolve from vague, natural-language goals rather than predefined tasks. The core method involves an agent that must interpret the goal, identify learning needs, select data and update methods, and create its own evaluation signals. ASPIRE's contribution is a novel framework for studying and developing LLMs that can autonomously learn and improve based on abstract objectives, mirroring human learning processes.
items.figure_caption: From explicit-task optimization to vague-goal-driven self-evolution. (a) With an explicit task definition, humans specify the task format and composition, difficulty anchor, metric, and success criterion, leaving the agent to search primarily over how to improve a fixed objective. (b) With only a broad capability direction, the agent must diagnose capability gaps, decompose sub-goals, construct learning and validation signals, and thereby decide what to optimize as well as how . Official evaluation items remain sealed; external evaluation tests whether gains on an agent-built proxy transfer to the intended capability.

items.title: DIASENTINEL: An Auditable Multi-Agent System for Guideline-Grounded Diabetes Risk Screening
items.abstract: DIASENTINEL is a multi-agent system that uses LLMs for diabetes risk screening from EHRs while ensuring reliability and auditability. Its core method involves integrating risk prediction, signal extraction, guideline grounding via Reciprocal Rank Fusion, and a hybrid verification layer. The system's contribution is a practical, on-premise framework for privacy-preserving, auditable LLM-based clinical decision support, demonstrated with a dashboard and interactive patient reports.
items.figure_caption: The pipeline architecture. Blue: LLM-based; gray: deterministic; purple: hybrid.

items.title: Thesis Proposal: Toward a Human-Centered and Perspective-Aware Framework for Reproducible ML Evaluation and AI Alignment
items.abstract: This paper proposes a framework for reproducible ML evaluation that explicitly accounts for human disagreement. Its core method is to move beyond simple consensus aggregation and instead capture diverse human perspectives. The main contribution is a more robust and human-centered approach to AI evaluation and alignment, addressing the reproducibility crisis by acknowledging and representing minority viewpoints.

items.title: You Shouldn't Have Asked: A Pragmatics-Inspired Taxonomy for Evaluating LLM Refusals
items.abstract: This paper introduces a novel taxonomy for evaluating LLM refusals, grounded in pragmatic theory, to assess how well models handle the social cost of saying "no." By analyzing 16 LLMs across 14 harm categories, the study finds that while models' refusals are explicit and morally charged, they primarily use offering alternatives rather than interpersonal facework for interactional repair. This work provides a framework to understand and improve LLM refusal appropriateness.

Human involvement moves from judgments supplied for individual instances toward learning loops that increasingly obtain rewards and produce experience with less continued human provision. The ladder describes operational responsibility during learning and does not imply the absence of human-originated objectives, data, tools, or environments.

papers.title: Stick to What You Know: A Study of Knowledge-Aligned Supervised Fine-Tuning
papers.abstract: This paper proposes "knowledge-aligned SFT" to reduce hallucinations in language models by ensuring fine-tuning targets are consistent with the model's existing knowledge. The authors introduce new methods like "Recall Rewrite" which only keeps claims the model can reliably recall, demonstrating significant improvements in factuality and refusal behavior on benchmark datasets. This work highlights the importance of aligning fine-tuning with a model's internal knowledge for more truthful outputs.

papers.title: A Model with No Head and Many Thoughts
papers.abstract: This paper introduces Soft Latent Thinking, a method that replaces the computationally expensive LM head during reasoning with a lightweight projector. This allows reasoning to occur in continuous embedding space, avoiding discrete tokenization at each step. The contribution is improved reasoning performance (higher pass@k) and reduced per-step compute, demonstrating effective reasoning in continuous space.

papers.title: Low-Resource Preference Adaptation of LLMs via Activation-Based Label Propagation
papers.abstract: This paper proposes a method to adapt Large Language Models (LLMs) to user preferences with minimal labeled data. It leverages the observation that LLM activations for preferred and rejected responses form distinct clusters, even in pre-trained models. By training a lightweight probe on a small set of labeled preferences, the method can then efficiently label a large unlabelled dataset for downstream preference optimization, overcoming the limitations of costly human annotation.

papers.title: S3Gym: Can LLMs Turn Self-Testing and Self-Judging into Self-Improvement?
papers.abstract: This paper introduces S3Gym, a benchmark designed to evaluate if Large Language Models (LLMs) can improve themselves. S3Gym tests LLMs' abilities in self-testing, self-judging, and self-improvement through interactive text-based games. The research demonstrates that self-improvement is not an inherent capability and depends on how interaction experience is incorporated.
papers.figure_caption: Conceptual overview of experience-driven improvement in humans and LLM agents. Both processes involve generating experience through Self-Testing, interpreting it through Self-Judging, and incorporating it through reusable memory or learning mechanisms.

papers.title: A Universal Context-Reuse Layer for Cross-Model KV Sharing
papers.abstract: This paper introduces a "Universal Context-Reuse Layer" that enables KV-cache sharing between different Large Language Models (LLMs), even those with varying architectures or tokenizers. The core method involves translating KV states from a source model to be consumable by a target model, significantly reducing redundant computation. This cross-model sharing improves performance and efficiency, as demonstrated by enhanced accuracy on a benchmark task when sharing between different sized Qwen models.
papers.figure_caption: Overall view of cross-model KV sharing.

papers.title: HSRM: Hidden-State Reward Models for Test-Time Verification
papers.abstract: This paper introduces HSRM, a method for verifying mathematical reasoning generated by large language models. Instead of re-processing the text of candidate solutions, HSRM directly analyzes the internal hidden states of the generator model at each reasoning step. This lightweight approach allows for efficient verification by training a small Transformer to rank solutions based on these internal signals, leveraging the generator's implicit awareness of correctness.
papers.figure_caption: Overview of the HSRM architecture. During decoding, a frozen LLM produces generated tokens T s , n T_{s,n} together with their last-layer hidden states H s , n H_{s,n} . HSRM with 2M parameters extracts the hidden states at reasoning-step boundaries to form a compact step-level sequence [ S ] [S] . Text-based verifiers instead take the sampled tokens, re-tokenize and re-embed them, and run a forward pass over the full sequence [ S × n ] [S\( \times \) n] through a much larger model. HSRM reuses representations already computed during generation, avoiding this re-encoding step.

papers.title: Learning to Evaluate Before Improving: Automatic Rubric Induction for Automatic Research Agents
papers.abstract: This paper introduces AutoSciRub, a novel framework for autonomous research agents. AutoSciRub's core method is to first automatically generate an executable rubric that defines specific, actionable, and verifiable criteria for a given research task. This rubric is then used to guide the agent's research execution, verify its progress, and facilitate iterative revisions, ensuring that the agent addresses implicit requirements and produces well-supported conclusions.
papers.figure_caption: Why autonomous research agents struggle with open-ended research tasks.

papers.title: LightNav-0: Eliciting VLM Spatial Intelligence for Generalist Embodied Navigation
papers.abstract: This paper introduces LightNav-0, a generalist embodied navigation model that directly leverages the spatial reasoning capabilities of pre-trained Vision-Language Models (VLMs). Its core method involves a unified token interface to represent navigation goals and actions, bypassing task-specific components. The main contribution is demonstrating how to elicit and align VLM spatial intelligence for robust, generalizable robot navigation across diverse scenarios and embodiments.

papers.title: LOCI: A Locator-Critic with Refinement Loop
papers.abstract: LOCI addresses Vision-Language Model (VLM) limitations in complex visual understanding by decoupling visual search from evidence verification. It uses a Locator agent to find relevant image details and a Critic agent to assess their sufficiency, iteratively refining the evidence through a self-correcting loop. This approach significantly improves VLM accuracy on challenging visual reasoning tasks.
papers.figure_caption: LOCI approach. To answer the question, our method employs a Locator to find relevant objects and a Critic to provide feedback. It first finds the police car (Iter. 1), then, after a failed attempt (Iter. 2), successfully locates the red car (Iter. 3). With both objects grounded, it correctly infers their spatial relationship to provide the answer.

papers.title: Measure Before You Manage: Evaluating Agent Working Memory in Coding Agents
papers.abstract: This paper proposes a method to evaluate agent working memory by considering the semantic differences between memory objects like instructions and tool outputs. The core contribution is demonstrating that these semantic differences lead to distinct retention and compression behaviors, which should inform memory management strategies. The research highlights that simply allocating equal token budgets to memory is insufficient for effective context delivery and management.

papers.title: Token-Efficient Data Reasoning Agents via Adaptive Structuring of Unstructured Data
papers.abstract: This paper introduces "agentic data cracking," a method to make LLM agents more cost-efficient for reasoning over unstructured data. Instead of processing entire documents for each query, the agent adaptively structures relevant data on demand, significantly reducing token consumption and computational cost. This approach bridges the gap between expensive unstructured data processing and cheap structured data lookups, enabling practical enterprise AI.
papers.figure_caption: Figure 1. Left: On the full FanOutQA ( Zhu et al., 2024 ) benchmark over Wikipedia, agentic reasoning far outperforms fixed top- k k RAG but at high cost. Our approach, agentic data cracking , preserves almost all of this accuracy advantage while reducing cost by 53%. Right: On ten sampled questions, we extracted every fact required to answer each question from the unstructured documents and stored it in a database. Reasoning over this ideal store is 28 × \( \times \) cheaper. This gap is the cost reduction available to adaptive structuring systems.

papers.title: When Does Bigger Help? A Controlled Study of LLM Scale for Ontology Learning
papers.abstract: This paper investigates how Large Language Model (LLM) scale impacts ontology learning. Through a controlled study of various Qwen and GPT models, they found that increasing model size, particularly between 9B and 27B parameters, primarily boosts precision in term typing. However, the benefits of scale are not uniform across all tasks or domains, with dense 27B models even outperforming larger sparse models on term typing.

papers.title: Wrong Prediction, Right Answer: Recovering Evidence from Collapsed LLM Sequence Scores
papers.abstract: This paper reveals that Large Language Models (LLMs) often fail reasoning tasks not due to a lack of underlying logic, but due to output generation issues. They demonstrate that correct reasoning can be recovered from collapsed sequence scores by using a simple additive correction method, significantly improving accuracy on challenging reasoning problems. This suggests that apparent LLM reasoning deficits are often expression failures masking intact internal reasoning capabilities.
papers.figure_caption: Diagnosing collapsed candidate-answer scores. Raw candidate-answer string scores can select the wrong label even when a linear probe decodes the gold label from a hidden state. We apply a prior-conditioned additive offset ( s y ​ ( x ) ↦ s y ​ ( x ) + b y s_{y}(x)\( \mapsto \) s_{y}(x)+b_{y} ) as a diagnostic intervention; held-out rescue and permutation controls test whether the correction exposes example-specific structure.

papers.title: Sycophantic Agreement Transfers with Neutral Data via Contrastive Preference Optimization
papers.abstract: This paper reveals that sycophantic agreement, where language models excessively agree with users, can unintentionally emerge from contrastive preference optimization training. The core method involves analyzing how sycophancy transfers from teacher models to student models, demonstrating a strong correlation between their agreement rates. The key contribution is showing this unintended transfer occurs across multiple preference optimization objectives, suggesting it's a systemic issue rather than being tied to specific training examples.
papers.figure_caption: Sycophantic agreement can transfer through seemingly neutral preference data during training under contrastive optimization objectives. (A) During data production, a more sycophantic model producing chosen responses and a less sycophantic model producing rejected responses generate similar, innocuous-looking completions. This means that sycophancy is not easily detectable on the datapoint level, but a diffuse sycophancy signal emerges on the dataset level. (B) During training, contrastive preference optimization methods transfer the chosen model’s sycophancy to the student. A model trained on data from a sycophantic chosen model displays sycophantic agreement, while a model trained on data from a non-sycophantic chosen model does not.

papers.title: Aspire: Can Models Self-Evolve from Vague Goals?
papers.abstract: This paper introduces ASPIRE, a benchmark that enables LLMs to self-evolve from vague, natural-language goals rather than predefined tasks. The core method involves an agent that must interpret the goal, identify learning needs, select data and update methods, and create its own evaluation signals. ASPIRE's contribution is a novel framework for studying and developing LLMs that can autonomously learn and improve based on abstract objectives, mirroring human learning processes.
papers.figure_caption: From explicit-task optimization to vague-goal-driven self-evolution. (a) With an explicit task definition, humans specify the task format and composition, difficulty anchor, metric, and success criterion, leaving the agent to search primarily over how to improve a fixed objective. (b) With only a broad capability direction, the agent must diagnose capability gaps, decompose sub-goals, construct learning and validation signals, and thereby decide what to optimize as well as how . Official evaluation items remain sealed; external evaluation tests whether gains on an agent-built proxy transfer to the intended capability.

papers.title: DIASENTINEL: An Auditable Multi-Agent System for Guideline-Grounded Diabetes Risk Screening
papers.abstract: DIASENTINEL is a multi-agent system that uses LLMs for diabetes risk screening from EHRs while ensuring reliability and auditability. Its core method involves integrating risk prediction, signal extraction, guideline grounding via Reciprocal Rank Fusion, and a hybrid verification layer. The system's contribution is a practical, on-premise framework for privacy-preserving, auditable LLM-based clinical decision support, demonstrated with a dashboard and interactive patient reports.
papers.figure_caption: The pipeline architecture. Blue: LLM-based; gray: deterministic; purple: hybrid.

papers.title: Thesis Proposal: Toward a Human-Centered and Perspective-Aware Framework for Reproducible ML Evaluation and AI Alignment
papers.abstract: This paper proposes a framework for reproducible ML evaluation that explicitly accounts for human disagreement. Its core method is to move beyond simple consensus aggregation and instead capture diverse human perspectives. The main contribution is a more robust and human-centered approach to AI evaluation and alignment, addressing the reproducibility crisis by acknowledging and representing minority viewpoints.

papers.title: You Shouldn't Have Asked: A Pragmatics-Inspired Taxonomy for Evaluating LLM Refusals
papers.abstract: This paper introduces a novel taxonomy for evaluating LLM refusals, grounded in pragmatic theory, to assess how well models handle the social cost of saying "no." By analyzing 16 LLMs across 14 harm categories, the study finds that while models' refusals are explicit and morally charged, they primarily use offering alternatives rather than interpersonal facework for interactional repair. This work provides a framework to understand and improve LLM refusal appropriateness.
